heroIntro: Marrying a second partner while a previous legal marriage remains legally subsisting is one of the most contentious issues in Bangladeshi family and criminal jurisprudence. Spouses frequently believe that an informal separation, a verbal pronouncement of talaq, or an affidavit of marriage entered into abroad terminates their marital ties. Under the Penal Code 1860, marrying again during the lifetime of a husband or wife without a prior, legally completed divorce constitutes the criminal offence of bigamy under Section 494, punishable with rigorous imprisonment up to seven years. Furthermore, for Muslim citizens, contracted polygamous unions without prior statutory permission violate Section 6 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961, triggering separate criminal penalties and immediate dower liabilities.

quickAnswer.title: Is Second Marriage Without Divorce Punishable in Bangladesh?
quickAnswer.text: Yes. Under Section 494 of the Penal Code 1860, anyone who marries a second time during the lifetime of their husband or wife while the earlier marriage remains legally valid is guilty of bigamy, punishable with imprisonment up to seven years and a fine. For Muslim husbands, contracting a second marriage without prior written permission from the statutory Arbitration Council is also a criminal offence under Section 6 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961, punishable with up to one year imprisonment or a fine up to 10,000 BDT, alongside the mandatory immediate payment of the entire dower (Denmohar) to the existing wife. For women of any faith, contracting a second marriage without a valid divorce is strictly bigamous under Section 494.
highlights: Section 494 Penal Code carries up to seven years imprisonment and a criminal fine.
A verbal talaq or informal separation does not constitute a legal divorce in Bangladesh.
Muslim husbands must obtain prior written permission from the Arbitration Council under MFLO Section 6.
Aggrieved spouses can file a Complaint Register (CR) case in the Judicial Magistrate Court.
points: Statutory Provisions: Section 494 Penal Code 1860 & Section 6 Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961.
Jurisdiction: Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) or Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) Court.

sections.title: 1. Core Elements of Bigamy under Section 494 of the Penal Code 1860
sections.content:
Section 494 of the Penal Code 1860 establishes that whoever, having a husband or wife living, marries in any case in which such marriage is void by reason of its taking place during the life of such husband or wife, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

To sustain a criminal conviction under Section 494, the prosecution or complainant must prove three essential factual ingredients beyond reasonable doubt:

  • First Marriage Subsisting: The accused had entered into a legally valid first marriage that was recognized under their personal law, and that first marriage had not been dissolved by a final, lawful decree of divorce or death.
  • Spouse Living: The first spouse was alive at the time the second marriage ceremony was performed.
  • Second Marriage Contracted: The accused entered into a second ceremony of marriage which would have been valid but for the subsistence of the prior marriage.

Under Schedule II of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898, an offence under Section 494 is classified as non-cognizable (meaning the police cannot register an FIR directly without a Magistrate's order), bailable, and compoundable by the aggrieved husband or wife with the permission of the court.

sections.title: 2. Muslim Husbands: Polygamy Restrictions under Section 6 of MFLO 1961
sections.content:
Under classical Islamic jurisprudence, a Muslim male is permitted up to four simultaneous wives under strict conditions of equal treatment. However, in Bangladesh, this religious permission is heavily regulated and restricted by Section 6 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 (MFLO).

Under Section 6(1) of the MFLO, no man, during the subsistence of an existing marriage, shall, except with the previous permission in writing of the Arbitration Council, contract another marriage, nor shall any such marriage contracted without such permission be registered under the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act 1974. The Arbitration Council consists of the Chairman of the local Union Parishad, Ward Councillor, or Cantonment Executive Officer, alongside a representative of the husband and each existing wife.

Permission is only granted under statutory rules upon proof that the existing wife is sterile, physically unfit for conjugal relations, or mentally incapacitated. If a husband marries without such written permission, he commits a direct statutory offence under Section 6(5) of the MFLO, rendering him liable to imprisonment up to one year or a fine up to 10,000 BDT, or both. For more details on husband and wife rights in polygamous marriages, review our analysis on polygamy law and second marriage in Bangladesh.

sections.title: 3. When a Wife Marries Without Divorce: Absolute Criminal Bigamy
sections.content:
While Muslim men have a conditional, heavily regulated statutory procedure under the MFLO to take a second wife, no personal law in Bangladesh—whether Muslim, Hindu, Christian, or Buddhist—permits a married woman to contract a second marriage while her first marriage subsists.

Polyandry is strictly void under all legal systems in Bangladesh. Consequently, if a married woman contracts a second marriage with another man without obtaining a final legal divorce from her first husband, that second marriage is completely void ab initio. The woman is directly punishable under Section 494 of the Penal Code with up to seven years of imprisonment.

Furthermore, the second husband, if he entered into the marriage knowing or having reason to believe that the woman was already the lawful wife of another living man, can be prosecuted as an abettor under Section 109 of the Penal Code or charged with adultery or fraudulent marriage under related provisions. sections.title: 4. The 90-Day Legal Rule: Why Verbal Talaq or Unregistered Divorce Fails
sections.content:
A widespread defense asserted by defendants facing Section 494 or Section 6 MFLO charges is that they had verbally pronounced talaq to their spouse, signed an informal separation paper on non-judicial stamp paper, or left the marital home months before the second marriage occurred. In Bangladeshi courts, this defense routinely collapses.

Under Section 7 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961, any husband who pronounces talaq in any form whatsoever must immediately give written notice of having done so to the Chairman of the Union Parishad or City Corporation, and must supply a copy thereof to the wife. Talaq does not take legal effect until the expiration of ninety (90) days from the day on which notice is delivered to the Chairman.

During these ninety days, the marriage remains fully legally intact. If a spouse marries before the formal 90-day period expires and before the Chairman issues the final Failure of Reconciliation Certificate, the prior marriage is still in force at law, rendering the second marriage strictly bigamous and illegal. For comprehensive procedural rules on divorce completion, review our step-by-step guide on divorce procedure in Bangladesh.

sections.title: 5. Procedure to File a CR Case Before the Judicial Magistrate Court
sections.content:
Because Section 494 of the Penal Code is non-cognizable, police officers will not register an FIR on a walk-in basis at a police station. Instead, the legal remedy requires the aggrieved spouse to file a Complaint Register (CR) case directly in the court of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) or Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) pursuant to Section 190 and Section 198 of the CrPC.

Under Section 198 of the CrPC, no court shall take cognizance of an offence under Chapter XX of the Penal Code (which includes Section 494) except upon a complaint made by some person aggrieved by the offence—specifically the first husband or first wife. The complainant, accompanied by an advocate, appears before the Magistrate to give sworn testimony under Section 200 CrPC.

The complainant must submit documentary evidence demonstrating the first marriage (the certified Nikahnama and marriage certificate) alongside proof of the second marriage (such as the second Nikahnama, wedding invitation cards, photographs, or witness affidavits). Upon examining the complainant, the Magistrate either issues a summons or warrant of arrest directly under Section 204 CrPC, or directs a local judicial inquiry under Section 202 CrPC. If you need assistance with Magistrate complaints, review our guide on criminal complaint procedures in Bangladesh.

sections.title: 6. Summary Matrix: Section 494 Penal Code vs. Section 6 MFLO 1961
sections.content:
Complainants and legal practitioners frequently evaluate whether to invoke the general Penal Code, the specific 1961 Family Ordinance, or both. The following comparative matrix outlines the operational differences:

Legal Dimension Section 494 Penal Code 1860 Section 6 Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961
Target Offence Bigamy (second marriage void due to subsisting first marriage) Contracting second marriage without Arbitration Council permission
Applicability All citizens (Muslim, Hindu, Christian, Buddhist) Muslim male citizens residing in Bangladesh or abroad
Maximum Imprisonment Imprisonment up to 7 years Imprisonment up to 1 year
Financial Fine Discretionary judicial fine Fine up to 10,000 BDT + immediate payment of entire dower
Cognizance Route CR Case filed by aggrieved spouse under Section 198 CrPC Complaint filed by existing wife or Arbitration Council Chairman
Validity of Second Union Completely void ab initio Marriage remains legally valid under personal law despite penalty

sections.title: 7. Financial Penalties: Immediate Dower Acceleration and Family Court Maintenance
sections.content:
Beyond criminal prosecution and jail terms, contracting an unauthorized second marriage triggers immediate, severe civil financial liabilities under Bangladeshi family law. The most significant of these is the automatic acceleration of the wife's dower (Denmohar).

Under Section 6(5)(a) of the MFLO 1961, any husband who enters into a second marriage without statutory permission must immediately pay the entire amount of the dower, whether prompt (Mu'ajjal) or deferred (Muwajjal), due to the existing wife or wives. Any deferred dower that was previously payable only upon divorce or the husband's death becomes immediately due and payable in full on the day of the second marriage ceremony.

If the husband fails to pay the dower immediately, the existing wife can file a suit in the Family Court under the Family Courts Act 2023 for recovery of the full dower amount along with past and ongoing monthly maintenance (Nafaqah). The Family Court possesses the power to attach the husband's bank accounts, garnish salary, seize immovable properties, and commit the husband to civil jail for non-payment. For a detailed guide on dower recovery, consult our resource on dower and maintenance recovery in Bangladesh.

sections.title: 8. Illustrative Scenario: Litigating an Unauthorized Second Marriage
sections.content:
To illustrate how bigamy litigation unfolds in the courts of Dhaka, consider the following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed).

A software architect living in the United Kingdom married a Bangladeshi woman in Dhaka in 2018, properly registering the Nikahnama. In 2023, while residing in London, the husband sent a brief WhatsApp message stating he was divorcing her, but never served written notice on the City Corporation Mayor or sent formal notices pursuant to Section 7 of the MFLO. Six months later, he returned to Dhaka and secretly married a second woman, registering a new marriage through a local Kazi.

Upon discovering the second marriage, the first wife engaged a Supreme Court advocate in Dhaka. The advocate verified that no divorce proceedings had ever been filed with the City Corporation Arbitration Council, rendering the first marriage fully subsisting under law. The advocate filed a Complaint Register (CR) case before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court under Section 494 of the Penal Code and Section 6(5) of the MFLO.

The CMM Court issued an arrest warrant against the husband. Simultaneously, the wife filed a Family Court suit for recovery of her 25 Lakh BDT dower and maintenance. Confronted with criminal detention and asset attachment, the husband was compelled to appear, deposit substantial financial security, and ultimately negotiate a comprehensive legal settlement granting the first wife full financial recovery.

sections.title: 9. Cross-Border & NRB Considerations: Foreign Marriages and Evidentiary Proof
sections.content:
Cross-border bigamy cases involving non-resident Bangladeshis in North America, Europe, and Australia are increasingly common. In many instances, a spouse who is legally married in Bangladesh travels abroad and enters into a civil marriage with a foreign national to obtain immigration residency or citizenship, falsely declaring themselves 'single' on visa applications.

If you are an aggrieved spouse residing in Bangladesh or abroad, securing admissible evidentiary proof is the cornerstone of criminal prosecution:

  • Procure the Original Certified Nikahnama: Obtain a certified copy (Nokol) of the first marriage record from the Kazi office or District Registrar, attested by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA).
  • Gather Proof of the Second Marriage: Obtain certified copies of the second marriage certificate, whether registered in Bangladesh or abroad (e.g., UK General Register Office or US County marriage records). Foreign documents must be authenticated and apostilled.
  • Verify Municipal Divorce Status: Request an official certificate from the relevant City Corporation Mayor or Union Parishad Chairman confirming that no Section 7 MFLO divorce notice was received or that reconciliation proceedings were never concluded.
  • Execute Power of Attorney for Court Filing: An overseas spouse does not need to travel to Bangladesh to initiate litigation; they can execute an embassy-attested Special Power of Attorney authorizing a lawyer or relative to file the CR complaint and Family Court suit.

For dedicated assistance with cross-border matrimonial litigation, consult our specialized divorce and family lawyer services in Bangladesh and criminal defense counsel.

faqs.question: Is second marriage without divorce a crime in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under Section 494 of the Penal Code 1860, marrying again while a first marriage subsists is the criminal offence of bigamy, punishable with imprisonment up to seven years and a fine. For Muslim men, contracting a second marriage without Arbitration Council permission also violates Section 6 of the MFLO 1961.

faqs.question: Can a Muslim husband marry a second wife legally in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: A Muslim husband may only marry a second wife if he submits a formal application and obtains prior written permission from the statutory Arbitration Council under Section 6 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961. Without this permission, the second marriage is a criminal offence.

faqs.question: What is the punishment under Section 6 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961?
faqs.answer: Under Section 6(5) of the MFLO, contracting a second marriage without written permission is punishable with simple imprisonment up to one year, or a fine up to 10,000 BDT, or both, alongside the immediate mandatory payment of the entire dower to the existing wife.

faqs.question: Does an informal separation or verbal talaq protect against bigamy charges?
faqs.answer: No. A verbal talaq has no legal effect under Section 7 of the MFLO 1961. A divorce only becomes legally final after written notice is served on the City Corporation or Union Parishad Chairman and ninety days elapse. Marrying before this period is bigamy.

faqs.question: Can a wife file a police FIR directly for bigamy in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: No. Section 494 of the Penal Code is non-cognizable under Schedule II of the CrPC. Police cannot register an FIR directly. The aggrieved spouse must file a Complaint Register (CR) case directly before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate or Chief Judicial Magistrate Court.

faqs.question: What happens to the wife's dower (Denmohar) if the husband marries a second wife?
faqs.answer: Under Section 6(5)(a) of the MFLO, the entire dower—both prompt and deferred—becomes immediately payable in full on the date of the second marriage. The existing wife can immediately file a Family Court suit to recover the full amount.

faqs.question: Is Section 494 Penal Code bailable in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Yes. Section 494 is classified as bailable and compoundable with the permission of the court under Schedule II of the CrPC. However, if warrants are issued and the accused absconds, the court may refuse bail until appearance or surrender.

faqs.question: Can an overseas wife sue her Bangladeshi husband for bigamy from abroad?
faqs.answer: Yes. An overseas wife can execute a Special Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission in her country of residence, empowering an advocate in Dhaka to file both the CR criminal case and Family Court financial claims.
